content.text: **Section 2 — Code quality review.** Skipping one trivial nit (3 source files vs 2 — ceremony, not a finding). Two real ones:

questions.question:
D6 / Issue 3 — Build identity (debug/nightly/production) already exists inside `SentryConfig`. Duplicating or importing it are both wrong. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-cq-build-identity-dry>

Project/branch/task: workroom @ master — `Core/SentryConfig.swift:67` defines `defaultEnvironment(nightly:debug:)` returning exactly "development"/"nightly"/"production", and `:76` defines `static let isDebugBuild`. Analytics needs the same three-way answer to decide whether to send anything at all.

ELI10: Two different features both need to know "is this a debug build, a nightly build, or the real app?" That logic is written once today, but it lives inside the crash-reporting file. If analytics reaches into that file it now depends on crash reporting for no reason; if it writes its own copy, you have the same rule in two places and they will drift the first time a fourth build identity appears.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the copies drift, and a nightly build starts reporting itself as production in one system while the other has it right — which is precisely the bug the nightly environment was added to fix (`SentryConfig.swift:57-63` documents WORKROOM-2B being indistinguishable from a production hang for exactly this reason).

Recommendation: A, because you asked me to flag repetition aggressively and this is a rule that already has one correct implementation — it just lives in the wrong file.

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

Pros / cons:
3A) Hoist to a shared `BuildIdentity`, both read it (recommended) (human: ~1h / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ One home for a rule that must never disagree with itself, and the existing `SentryConfigTests` keeps covering it
  ✅ A future fourth identity is one edit, and both systems get it without anyone remembering to sync them
  ❌ Touches a file that currently works, so it is a small refactor riding along with a feature change
3B) Analytics calls `SentryConfig.isDebugBuild` directly (human: ~5 min / CC: ~1 min)
  ✅ Zero new code and zero refactor risk — both members are already internal and reachable today
  ✅ Cannot drift, since there is still exactly one implementation being read from two places
  ❌ Analytics now depends on a crash-reporting type, so deleting or gating Sentry later breaks analytics for no reason
3C) Analytics writes its own `#if DEBUG` check (human: ~5 min / CC: ~1 min)
  ✅ Fully independent — the two systems can be changed or removed without touching each other at all
  ✅ Reads locally without the reader having to know what `SentryConfig` is
  ❌ This is the exact repetition you want flagged, and the two copies will disagree eventually

Net: the rule exists and is correct; the only question is whether it keeps living in the crash-reporting file.

options.label: Hoist to shared BuildIdentity
options.description: New Core/BuildIdentity.swift owns debug/nightly/production. SentryConfig.defaultEnvironment and Analytics both read it. Existing SentryConfigTests move with it. (recommended)

options.label: Analytics reads SentryConfig
options.description: No refactor. Analytics calls SentryConfig.isDebugBuild / defaultEnvironment directly. Couples analytics to the crash-reporting type.

options.label: Analytics keeps its own check
options.description: Independent #if DEBUG plus ReleaseChannel.isNightlyBuild inside Analytics. No coupling, but the rule now exists twice.

questions.question:
D7 / Issue 4 — The POST fires at launch, which is exactly when the network is least likely to be up. What happens when it fails? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-cq-send-failure-policy>

Project/branch/task: workroom @ master — D4 chose a self-hosted endpoint, so we own the send. The plan never states a failure policy. Given as fixed either way: the send is off the main thread and a failure is never shown to the user.

ELI10: The single event fires seconds after the app opens. A very common way people open this app is lidding open a laptop, where wifi has not reconnected yet. If a failed send is simply dropped, you do not lose a random sample — you systematically lose the "just woke my machine" launches, which is probably a large slice of real use, and every percentage you compute is skewed by it in a way the data cannot reveal.

Stakes if we pick wrong: drop-on-failure quietly under-counts a whole category of launch, and you would conclude something about your users from data biased by their network timing. Go too far the other way and you are writing a queue file to the user's disk — the device storage that D3 and D4 deliberately eliminated.

Recommendation: B, because launch-time network failure is systematic rather than random, and one in-memory retry fixes it without putting a single byte on the user's disk.

Completeness: A=5/10, B=8/10, C=10/10

Pros / cons:
4A) Fire and forget — one attempt, failure dropped silently (human: ~30 min / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Simplest possible sink, nothing to get wrong, and provably writes nothing to the user's machine
  ✅ A dropped event costs nothing operationally since there is no identity and nothing to reconcile
  ❌ Systematically loses cold-wake launches, biasing every derived percentage in an undetectable direction
4B) One in-memory retry after a short delay, then drop (recommended) (human: ~1h / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Covers the real systematic case — wifi arriving a few seconds after launch — for about ten lines of code
  ✅ Still writes nothing to disk, so the privacy posture from D3 and D4 is completely intact
  ❌ Keeps one event in memory briefly and needs a test for the retry path, so it is not quite free
4C) On-disk queue, retried across launches (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Highest delivery — an offline user's events all arrive eventually, so no launch category is lost
  ✅ Standard shape for analytics SDKs, so the behaviour is well understood and easy to reason about
  ❌ Writes analytics state to the user's device, reintroducing exactly the storage that D3 and D4 removed

Net: drop-on-failure is not neutral — it loses a specific kind of launch, not a random one.

options.label: One in-memory retry, then drop
options.description: Attempt, and on failure retry once after ~10-30s from memory only. Then drop silently. Nothing touches disk. Covers the cold-wake-no-wifi case. (recommended)

options.label: Fire and forget
options.description: Single attempt, failure dropped silently. Simplest sink possible, provably no device storage, accepts the cold-wake bias.

options.label: On-disk queue with retry
options.description: Persist unsent events, retry across launches. Best delivery. Writes analytics state to the user's disk, reintroducing the storage D3/D4 removed.

content.text:
**Section 3 — Test review.** Framework: XCTest via `make app-test` (`WorkroomAppTests`), separate `WorkroomAppUITests` scheme. Traced every branch of the reduced design:

```
CODE PATHS                                              USER FLOWS
[~] Core/BuildIdentity.swift  (hoisted from SentryConfig)   [+] Fresh install, zero projects
  └── environment(nightly:debug:)                             └── [GAP] launch emits zero-count snapshot
      ├── [★★★ TESTED] debug→development                  [+] User opts out in Settings
      ├── [★★★ TESTED] nightly→nightly                       ├── [GAP] [→E2E] toggle flips + persists
      └── [★★★ TESTED] release→production                    └── [GAP]        next launch sends nothing
          (SentryConfigTests move with it — REGRESSION)   [+] Cold-wake launch, wifi not up
                                                            ├── [GAP] retry fires once, then drops
[+] Core/AnalyticsEvent.swift                               └── [GAP] no user-visible error, no log spam
  ├── CountBucket.of(Int)                                 [+] ⌘N second window
  │   ├── [GAP] 0  ← NO BUCKET DEFINED (Issue 5)            └── [GAP] no second event
  │   ├── [GAP] boundaries 1 / 2 / 5 / 6 / 20 / 21
  │   └── [GAP] negative — unreachable, assert anyway
  └── [GAP] every case encodes to a stable name

[+] Core/Analytics.swift
  └── track(_:)
      ├── [GAP] gate off      → sink never called
      ├── [GAP] gate on+debug → Noop sink, nothing sent
      ├── [GAP] gate on+release → real sink
      └── [GAP] under XCTest  → Noop sink

[~] Core/AppStore.swift:2344  load()
      ├── [GAP] first success        → emits once
      ├── [GAP] reloadIfStale later  → does NOT emit
      ├── [GAP] second window's load → does NOT emit
      └── [GAP] load FAILED          → ??? undefined (Issue 6)

[+] HTTPSink  (Stage 2)
      ├── [GAP] 200 → done, no retry
      ├── [GAP] non-2xx → one retry → drop
      ├── [GAP] transport error → one retry → drop
      ├── [GAP] retry succeeds → done
      └── [GAP] quit before retry → dropped, no crash

COVERAGE: 3/24 paths tested (13%)  |  Code paths: 3/18 (17%)  |  User flows: 0/6 (0%)
QUALITY: ★★★:3  |  GAPS: 21 (2 E2E, 0 eval)
```

**REGRESSION (mandatory, no question asked):** hoisting `defaultEnvironment` out of `SentryConfig` modifies working behavior. `SentryConfigTests` moves to `BuildIdentityTests` and keeps asserting the same three outputs, **and** a test pins that `SentryConfig` still tags nightly as `nightly` — that mislabelling is the documented WORKROOM-2B failure (`SentryConfig.swift:57-63`).

Two gaps need your decision:

questions.question:
D8 / Issue 5 — `CountBucket` has no bucket for zero, and zero is a real, common state. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-test-countbucket-zero>

Project/branch/task: workroom @ master — the plan defines buckets `.one`, `.few` (2-5), `.some` (6-20), `.many` (21+). Nothing covers 0. A fresh install has zero projects, and `add-project` exists specifically so the app can show a registered project with zero workrooms.

ELI10: The event reports how many projects and workrooms someone has, rounded into ranges so it cannot identify anyone. But there is no range for "none." Whatever the code does with zero — crash, or quietly report "one" — it is wrong, and "reports one" is the dangerous kind of wrong because it is invisible: every brand-new install would look like an install that is actually being used.

Stakes if we pick wrong: you cannot distinguish "downloaded it and never added a project" from "added one project and uses it" — which is the single most important question for a tool at this stage, since it is the difference between an activation problem and a retention problem.

Recommendation: A, because zero is not an edge case here, it is the state every user is in for their first few minutes, and it answers a question none of the other buckets can.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=4/10

Pros / cons:
5A) Add an explicit `.none` bucket for 0 (recommended) (human: ~15 min / CC: ~2 min)
  ✅ Makes the activation question answerable — how many installs never register a single project
  ✅ Removes an undefined input from a pure function, so the boundary test suite is actually complete
  ❌ One more enum case to carry, and a zero-project launch is now distinguishable from a one-project one
5B) Clamp 0 into `.one` and document it (human: ~5 min / CC: ~1 min)
  ✅ No new case, and the function is total — every integer maps somewhere defined
  ✅ Slightly coarser data is marginally friendlier to anonymity than a distinct zero signal
  ❌ Silently merges "never started" with "actively using one project", losing the activation signal entirely
5C) Assert 0 is unreachable and trap in debug (human: ~10 min / CC: ~2 min)
  ✅ Surfaces the assumption loudly rather than encoding a guess about what zero means
  ❌ It IS reachable — a fresh install has no projects — so this ships a crash on the most common first-run state
  ❌ Even if guarded to debug builds only, it makes the first-run path the one path least likely to be tested

Net: zero is the first state every user is in, and right now the schema has nothing to say about it.

options.label: Add explicit .none bucket
options.description: CountBucket gains .none for 0. Boundary tests cover 0/1/2/5/6/20/21. Makes "installed but never added a project" visible as an activation signal. (recommended)

options.label: Clamp 0 into .one
options.description: No new case, function stays total, documented. Merges never-started with actively-using-one — activation signal lost.

options.label: Assert 0 unreachable
options.description: Precondition/assert in debug builds. Surfaces the assumption — but zero IS reachable on first run.

Sending the event anyway records "this person has zero projects," which is a lie, and it lands in the exact bucket you just added in Issue 5 to measure whether new users ever get started. A handful of failed loads would look like an activation problem that does not exist.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the one metric you added specifically to answer "do people get started" is silently contaminated by unrelated CLI read failures, and there is no field in the data that would let you notice.

Recommendation: A. B and C score higher on completeness, but the coverage they add measures CLI health, not product usage — that is a different question and belongs in a separate mechanism, not bolted onto the metric it would corrupt.

Completeness: A=7/10, B=9/10, C=10/10

6A) Emit only on a successful load; a failed first load means no event this launch (recommended) (human: ~15 min / CC: ~3 min)

  ✅ One clear rule with one obvious test, and the once-flag stays unset so a later successful reload can still emit
  ❌ Launches where the CLI is broken vanish from the data entirely, so total launch counts run slightly low
6B) Emit anyway with a `load_failed: true` flag (human: ~30 min / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ You learn how often the project list actually fails in the field, which nothing currently measures
  ✅ No launch is missing from the dataset, so launch totals stay honest
  ❌ Every consumer of the count fields must remember to filter on the flag, and one that forgets gets a wrong answer
6C) Emit the snapshot on success, plus a separate minimal failure event (human: ~1h / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Both questions answered cleanly with no shared fields that could be misread by a careless query
  ✅ The failure event needs no counts at all, so it cannot contaminate anything
  ❌ Two event types in a schema designed around one, for a failure mode nobody has reported yet

Net: a failed read must not be recorded as a user with nothing — the only question is whether the failure gets its own signal.

# Product analytics for the Workroom macOS app

## Context

The app has **no product analytics**. Sentry is linked and running (`Core/SentryConfig.swift`,
started at `WorkroomApp.swift:19`) with crash reporting, app-hang tracking, tracing, profiling and
metrics — but it answers "what broke", never "what gets used". Tracing/profiling are effectively
dead weight today: the app opens no transactions (`TODOS.md:1719`).

That gap costs real decisions. Nothing tells us whether jj or git dominates, whether the inspector's
Files/PR panes earn their code, whether side-by-side diff is used, how many workrooms a real user
keeps, or whether the `pre` channel has anyone on it. GA scoping is currently guesswork.

**Non-goal — the CLI is never instrumented.** This is macOS-app-only. The Go CLI is a standalone
terminal tool and the only option on Linux/Windows; it gets nothing, including the copy the app
bundles and symlinks into PATH via `CommandLineInstaller`. Someone running `workroom` in a terminal
is invisible to this feature by construction.

## The shape, and why

Everything here follows from one decision: **no identity**. No install ID, no device ID, no vendor
client ID. That choice cascades — and the cascade is the design:

```
no identity
  ├─→ no retention/DAU              (accepted: event counts only)
  ├─→ nothing written to the user's disk
  │     └─→ no ePrivacy "storage or access on terminal equipment" exposure
  │           └─→ opt-out default-on is defensible
  │                 └─→ no first-run consent modal needed
  ├─→ no on-disk retry queue        (in-memory retry only)
  └─→ no third-party SDK            (they all mint their own client ID)
        └─→ self-hosted endpoint
```

The ePrivacy consent rule covers *any* non-essential storage or access on a user's device, and
analytics is explicitly not "strictly necessary". The install ID was the thing that triggered it —
not the events. Removing it is what makes the rest of the posture hold together.

**Every third-party SDK reintroduces it.** TelemetryDeck's own docs: it "will create a user
identifier for your user that is specific to app installation and device." So a vendor is not a
neutral choice here — it silently undoes the decision. Hence self-hosted.

## Design

### Stage 1 — nothing leaves the machine

Full schema, consent gate, Settings toggle, `os.Logger` sink. Verifiable end to end locally; a bad
schema never reaches a server. Acceptance test for the stage: `nettop` shows zero new outbound
connections.

### Stage 2 — the self-hosted sink

One `AnalyticsSink` conformance we own: a `URLSession` POST to our own endpoint. Hard constraints,
non-negotiable and testable:

- **Never persists or transmits any per-install or per-device identifier.**
- **Writes nothing to disk.** No queue, no cache, no ID.
- **One in-memory retry** after a short delay, then silent drop. Launch is exactly when the network
  is least likely to be up (cold wake, wifi reconnecting), so a single-attempt send would
  systematically lose that whole category of launch rather than a random sample.
- Off the main thread. Never surfaces an error to the user.

### The event — one snapshot, no action events

```
  WorkroomApp.init ──► (too early: no AppStore, no project list)
                             │
  AppStore.load() ───────────┴──► success? ──no──► emit nothing, once-flag stays UNSET
   (Core/AppStore.swift:2344)         │             (a later successful reload may still emit)
                                     yes
                                      │
                          Analytics.trackLaunchSnapshot()
                                      │
                    ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
              hasSentLaunchSnapshot?                    │
                    │ true                              │ false → set it
                 return                                 │
                                                        ▼
                                        Defaults[.analyticsEnabled]? ──off──► return
                                                        │ on
                                        BuildIdentity ──debug/XCTest──► NoopSink
                                                        │ release/nightly
                                                        ▼
                                            Stage 1: OSLogSink
                                            Stage 2: HTTPSink (off-main, 1 retry)
```

The static `hasSentLaunchSnapshot` flag is load-bearing: `WorkroomApp.swift:54-59` documents that
SwiftUI "mints one window — and one fresh `AppStore` — per `WindowSeed`", and ⌘N opens a new seed.
Without the flag, launch counts inflate with ⌘N and window restoration, and with no identity there
is nothing to deduplicate on server-side.

`app_launch` carries: app version, `ReleaseChannel` subscription, build identity, macOS version,
arch, project count (bucketed), workroom count (bucketed), VCS mix (has-git / has-jj — free from
`Project.vcs`, `Models.swift:53`), theme family, diff view mode, inspector open + section,
menu-bar item on/off.

### The schema is a closed enum

`AnalyticsEvent` is an enum with associated values; `AnalyticsValue` is `.string` (from a closed
set) / `.int` / `.bool`; `CountBucket` is `.none` (0) / `.one` / `.few` (2–5) / `.some` (6–20) /
`.many` (21+). This is the load-bearing decision: it is a **compile-time** guarantee that a repo
path, project name, branch, bookmark, workroom label or terminal line cannot be attached to an
event. A `[String: Any]` API would make that a review-discipline problem forever.

`.none` exists because zero is not an edge case — it is the state every user is in for their first
few minutes, and it is the only way to tell "installed but never added a project" (activation) from
"has one project and uses it" (retention). Clamping 0 into `.one` would merge them invisibly.

Never sent: paths, project/workroom/branch/bookmark names, labels, commit messages, file names,
terminal content, or anything derived from them. `SecretRedactor` is not the control — it targets
secret shapes in terminal output; the closed schema is the control.

### Consent

One key in `Core/DefaultsKeys.swift`:

```swift
static let analyticsEnabled = Key<Bool>("analyticsEnabled", default: true)
```

Toggle lives in the **existing** `GeneralSettingsPane` (`Views/SettingsView.swift:178`) — no new
Settings pane. The gate is checked before the sink is constructed: off means no network client is
ever built. Same contract as `loadRemoteAvatars` (`DefaultsKeys.swift:101`, "off ⇒ NO avatar image
request is made"), which is the house precedent to match.

### `BuildIdentity` — hoisted, not duplicated

`SentryConfig.defaultEnvironment(nightly:debug:)` (`SentryConfig.swift:67`) already returns exactly
`development`/`nightly`/`production`, and `isDebugBuild` sits at `:76`. Analytics needs the same
three-way answer. Move both to `Core/BuildIdentity.swift`; `SentryConfig` and `Analytics` both read
it. One home for a rule that must never disagree with itself — a nightly build reporting itself as
production in one system and correctly in the other is precisely the WORKROOM-2B confusion
documented at `SentryConfig.swift:57-63`.

## Files

**New**
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/BuildIdentity.swift` — hoisted from `SentryConfig`
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/AnalyticsEvent.swift` — closed enum, `AnalyticsValue`, `CountBucket`
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/Analytics.swift` — façade, gate, once-flag, sink selection, `AnalyticsSink`
  protocol + `NoopSink` + `OSLogSink`
- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/BuildIdentityTests.swift`, `AnalyticsTests.swift`
- Stage 2 only: `Core/AnalyticsHTTPSink.swift`

**Edited**
- `Core/DefaultsKeys.swift` — one key
- `Core/SentryConfig.swift` — reads `BuildIdentity` instead of owning it
- `Core/AppStore.swift:2344` — emit at the end of a successful `load`
- `Views/SettingsView.swift:178` — toggle in `GeneralSettingsPane`, with an `accessibilityIdentifier`
- `macapp/README.md`, root `README.md` — a privacy/telemetry section

Adding files needs `make app-generate` (XcodeGen expands the source glob into the gitignored
`.xcodeproj`).

## Tests

Aim is every branch. From the review's coverage trace:

**`BuildIdentityTests`** — REGRESSION, mandatory: the three environment outputs survive the hoist,
and `SentryConfig` still tags nightly as `nightly`.

**`AnalyticsTests`**
- `CountBucket` boundaries: 0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 20, 21 — and that 0 maps to `.none`, not `.one`
- every `AnalyticsEvent` case encodes to a stable name (a rename is a data-contract break)
- gate off ⇒ spy sink never called, and no network client constructed
- gate on + debug build ⇒ `NoopSink`
- gate on + under XCTest ⇒ `NoopSink`
- gate on + release ⇒ real sink
- once-flag: first emit fires, second call is a no-op
- failed load ⇒ no emit **and** the once-flag stays unset, so a later success still emits

**Stage 2 `AnalyticsHTTPSinkTests`** (via a `URLProtocol` stub)
- 200 ⇒ done, no retry
- non-2xx ⇒ exactly one retry ⇒ drop
- transport error ⇒ exactly one retry ⇒ drop
- retry succeeds ⇒ done
- teardown before the retry fires ⇒ dropped, no crash

**XCUITest** (scoped to the new class only — never the full `WorkroomAppUITests` suite, and
`make app-uitest` ignores `APP_TEST_FLAGS`, so call `xcodebuild -only-testing:<Class>/<method>`)
- the General-pane toggle flips and persists — matched by `accessibilityIdentifier`, since XCUITest
  cannot match a `Form` `Toggle` by label

## Failure modes

| Path | Realistic failure | Test? | Handled? | User sees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Emit at `load` | Fires twice via ⌘N | yes (once-flag) | yes | nothing (correct) |
| Emit at `load` | Load failed ⇒ reports zero projects | yes | yes (no emit) | nothing (correct) |
| `CountBucket` | 0 projects undefined | yes | yes (`.none`) | nothing |
| HTTP sink | Cold-wake, no wifi | yes | yes (1 retry, drop) | nothing — silent by design |
| HTTP sink | Endpoint down for days | yes | yes (drop) | nothing |
| Gate | Toggle off but client still built | yes | yes | nothing |

No critical gaps: every failure mode above has both a test and explicit handling, and every one is
deliberately silent — analytics must never interrupt the user.

## NOT in scope

- **CLI instrumentation** — explicit non-goal, per above.
- **Action events** (`workroom_created`, `pane_split`, `vcs_action`, …) — deferred. The launch
  snapshot answers the questions actually asked; actions are a second increment once the pipe works.

D10 / CROSS-MODEL TENSION — Codex says the launch snapshot cannot answer the questions it exists for. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-tension-snapshot-vs-actions>

Project/branch/task: workroom @ master — Step 0 reduced the plan to snapshot-only and you chose that in D3. Codex attacks that reduction directly, and I think it lands.

ELI10: The snapshot reads settings at startup — which inspector tab is selected, which diff layout is saved. That tells you what someone's preferences are, not whether they ever open those panes. "Files pane setting is selected" and "Files pane gets used" are different facts, and only the second one answers whether that code earns its place. Codex also notes that with no identity, someone who launches ten times a day counts ten times more than someone who launches once, so every percentage is weighted by launch frequency rather than by person.

Stakes if we pick wrong: you build the pipe, ship it, wait a month, and the data still cannot tell you whether the Files pane is used — because it never measured use. The context I might be missing is your actual tolerance: for a rough "is anyone on the pre channel, is jj real" read, launch-weighted state is genuinely enough, and Codex may be holding this to a standard you do not need.

Recommendation: A. Codex is right that state-at-launch is not usage, and coarse action events are barely more work than the snapshot once the gate, schema and sink already exist — which is the whole cost centre. Adding two or three counters is a small delta on top.

Completeness: A=9/10, B=6/10, C=10/10

Pros / cons:
10A) Replace the snapshot with a few coarse identity-free action events (recommended) (human: ~2 days / CC: ~40 min)
  ✅ Measures what was actually asked — pane opened, diff mode switched, workroom created, VCS action run
  ✅ Nearly free once the gate, schema and sink exist, since those are the expensive parts and they are unchanged
  ❌ Loses the cheap population facts the snapshot gave for free, like OS spread and project-count distribution
10B) Keep the snapshot as planned, accept that it measures state (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Smallest possible first increment, one emit site, one event type, nothing to sequence
  ✅ Population facts — OS, channel, VCS mix, counts — are real answers the snapshot genuinely does provide
  ❌ Cannot answer the feature-usage questions that motivated the work, and you will not find that out for a month
10C) Snapshot AND coarse action events in the same increment (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1h)
  ✅ Population facts plus real usage signal, so no question in the original list goes unanswered
  ✅ One consent conversation and one pipe instead of shipping analytics to users twice
  ❌ Widens the first increment right after Step 0 deliberately narrowed it, and more emit sites means more leak surface

Net: the snapshot measures configuration; the questions are about behaviour. Decide which one you are actually buying.

D11 — Codex is right that "self-hosted endpoint" is one bullet where there is an entire system. <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-stage2-is-a-system>

Project/branch/task: workroom @ master — D4 chose self-hosted over a vendor SDK. The plan describes the client half in detail and the server half in a sentence.

ELI10: Right now the plan says "POST to our own endpoint." That endpoint does not exist. Making it real means: something running somewhere, a way to stop strangers spamming it, a version field so old app versions do not poison the data when the schema changes, storage, a rule for how long data is kept and how it gets deleted, and something to actually look at the numbers. That is a backend project, and it does not get designed properly in the last five minutes of a client-side review. There is also a sequencing problem nobody has named: Stage 1 ships a Settings switch labelled "Send anonymous usage data" that sends nothing, which is a lie to the user.

Stakes if we pick wrong: either you sketch a backend badly here and build the wrong one, or Stage 1 ships a toggle that misrepresents what the app does.

Recommendation: B. The deferred half is a different kind of work, not a smaller amount of the same work — that is the legitimate reason to scope it out rather than rush it. And option C deserves a real look during that pass: self-hosted Aptabase is open source and you run it, which keeps D4's "no vendor holds the data" property while skipping the storage and dashboard build entirely.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=9/10

Pros / cons:
11A) Design the endpoint now as part of this plan (human: ~1 week / CC: ~2h)
  ✅ One coherent design covering client and server, with nothing left implicit between them
  ✅ Forces the retention and deletion policy to be decided before any data exists to be governed by it
  ❌ A backend designed as an appendix to a client review is the one most likely to be rebuilt later
11B) Land Stage 1 on master WITHOUT the Settings toggle; plan the endpoint separately (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~25 min)
  ✅ Schema, gate, buckets and emit sites get built and tested for real while sending nothing anywhere
  ✅ No user ever sees a switch that controls nothing, because the toggle ships with the thing it controls
  ❌ Analytics produce zero answers until a second piece of work happens, which may be a while
11C) Re-evaluate self-hosted Aptabase before building anything (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Open source and you host it, so no vendor holds the data — D4's actual concern is satisfied
  ✅ Skips building storage, aggregation and dashboards, which is most of what Codex says is missing
  ❌ Needs verification that its SDK does not mint a device identifier, which is exactly what D4 ruled out

Net: the client half is ready to build; the server half is a separate project wearing a one-line disguise.

# README

1	# CLAUDE.md
2	
3	This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
4	
5	## Commands
6	
7	| Task | Command |
8	| --- | --- |
9	| Install + prepare DB + start dev server | `bin/setup` |
10	| Start dev server (Rails + Caddy HTTPS via `rails_caddy_dev`) | `bin/dev` |
11	| Run a Sidekiq worker (background jobs) | `bin/jobs` |
12	| Run full test suite | `bin/rails test` |
13	| Run JS tests | `bun test` |
14	| Run a single file | `bin/rails test test/models/concerns/stateful_test.rb` |
15	| Run a single test by name | `bin/rails test path/to/file.rb -n /pattern/` |
16	| Lint | `bin/rubocop` |
17	| Auto-correct lint | `bin/rubocop -A` |
18	| Security: gem audit | `bin/bundler-audit` |
19	| Security: code analysis | `bin/brakeman` |
20	| Full CI (setup + rubocop + audits + tests + seed replant) | `bin/ci` |
21	| Reset + reseed DB | `bin/rails db:reset` / `bin/rails db:seed:replant` |
22	
23	`bin/setup` accepts `--reset` (drop+recreate DB) and `--skip-server` (don't `exec bin/dev` after).
24	
25	Dev mail is intercepted by `letter_thief` and viewable at `/letter_thief`. A demo route mounts at
26	`/demo` in development only.
27	
28	## Stack
29	
30	* **Ruby 4.0.3 / Rails 8.1.3 / PostgreSQL.** Schema defaults all primary keys to UUID v7
31	  (`uuidv7()` Postgres function). The default is applied by
32	  `config/initializers/uuid_v7_defaults.rb`, which patches `SchemaStatements#create_table` /
33	  `add_reference` so migrations don't have to repeat `id: :uuid, default: -> { "uuidv7()" }`.
34	* **Sidekiq + Redis** for background jobs (`config.active_job.queue_adapter = :sidekiq` in
35	  production; run a worker locally with `bin/jobs`). Action Cable uses `async` in development and
36	  `redis` in production. Cache is `:memory_store` in dev, `:null_store` in test — no Solid
37	  adapters. Single Postgres DB per environment.
38	* **Phlex + Phlexible** for views. **No ERB.** Views are Ruby classes in `app/views/<controller>/`,
39	  and controllers auto-render via `Phlexible::Rails::ActionController::ImplicitRender`. Reusable UI
40	  lives under `app/components/<component>/`. `layout false` is set globally on
41	  `ApplicationController`; layout composition is handled by `Phlexible::Rails::AutoLayout`.
42	* **Proscenium** for assets, with sideloaded CSS modules. Bundling is JS-side via **bun**.
43	  Components follow a **zeitwerk nsfile convention**: each component lives in
44	  `app/components/<namespace>/<name>/` and colocates `ns.rb`, `ns.module.css`, `ns.js`, and
45	  `ns.test.js`. The directory itself is the namespace, so the Ruby class is `Components::Foo::Bar`
46	  (no `::Component` suffix) and render calls look like `render Components::Card::List.new(...)`.
47	* **Auth is passwordless** — magic link + 6-digit OTP, delivered via mailer
48	  (`OneTimePasscode.generate_for`). Sessions live in `sessions` table. `Current.session` /
49	  `Current.user` are `ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes`. The `Authentication` concern is included
50	  in `ApplicationController`; controllers opt out with `allow_unauthenticated_access`.
51	* **Org membership gate** — `ControllerConcerns::EnsureMembership` redirects authenticated users
52	  with no `OrganisationMembership` to `new_organisation_path`. Opt out with
53	  `allow_without_membership`.
54	* **Tests** — minitest + maxitest, parallelized at the worker count. `with_model` for throwaway
55	  models (use it when testing concerns), `fixture_kit` (in `test/fixture_kit/default.rb`) instead
56	  of YAML fixtures — recreated once per test run via `FixtureKit.define { ... }`. Capybara is
57	  available for system tests.
58	
59	## Architecture
60	
61	### Domain model
62	
63	`User` ↔ `OrganisationMembership` ↔ `Organisation` → `Project` → `Card`. Membership is enforced as
64	a controller-level redirect, not at the model layer. Cards optionally belong to a project.
65	
66	### Stateful concern (event-sourced state machine)
67	
68	`app/models/concerns/stateful.rb` adds a state machine that **doesn't store state on the model
69	row**. Every transition is appended to the polymorphic `transitions` table; the row flagged
70	`most_recent: true` defines `current_state`, falling back to `initial_state` when no transitions
71	exist. Read its module-level docs before using or extending it — the design intent (audit trail,
72	frozen graph, `:any` wildcard, opaque `metadata` jsonb) is documented inline. `Card` is the first
73	adopter; its graph treats every workflow lane (`triage`, `plan:*`, `dev:*`, `qa:*`) as `:any`
74	(free movement) and only `closed:*` as terminal.
75	
76	### CRUD controllers
77	
78	`ControllerConcerns::Crud` provides a generic `index`/`show`/`new`/`create`/`edit`/`update`/
79	`destroy` set wired through the `responders` gem. Concrete controllers (e.g. `CardsController`)
80	just declare `creatable_params`/`updatable_params` and `collection`. `params[:validate_only]`
81	short-circuits create/update for client-side validation flows.
82	
83	### View resolution
84	
85	`ApplicationController#phlex_view_path` maps `controller_path/action_name` → `views/.../action`,
86	so `cards#index` renders `Views::Cards::Index`. View classes inherit from `Views::Application`,
87	which mixes in Proscenium asset sideloading + CSS modules + Phlexible's auto-layout. Controller
88	instance variables flow into views via `Phlexible::Rails::ControllerVariables` + the
89	`controller_variable :name` declaration in the view class.
90	
91	## Conventions
92	
93	These are enforced by `.rubocop.yml` (`TargetRubyVersion: 4.0`, `Max: 100`). Read the file —
94	deviations from defaults matter:
95	
96	* **`# frozen_string_literal: true` is implicit** (`StringLiteralsFrozenByDefault: true`). Don't
97	  add the magic comment; rubocop will require it gone.
98	* **Disabled syntax** (`Style/DisableSyntax`): no `unless`, no `and`/`or`/`not` keywords, no
99	  numbered block parameters (`_1`, `_2`). Use `if` (with restructured/negated conditions or a
100	  positively-named flag), `&&`/`||`/`!`, and named block params or the `it` shorthand.
101	* **Modern Ruby syntax is the project style** — endless method definitions (`def foo = bar`),
102	  hash value shorthand (`{ user:, role: }`), pattern matching where it clarifies. Card and the
103	  Stateful concern are reference examples.
104	* **Phlex views use block element methods** — `div { ... }`, `h1 { card.title }`, not `tag.div(...)`.
105	* **Comments wrap to ~99 chars**, not 80. Match the code line-length budget.
106	* **Documentation cop is off**, but module/class docstrings are still expected on non-trivial
107	  shared infrastructure (see Stateful for the bar).
108	* **Metrics cop is off** — long methods are tolerated when they read well.

**codaset facts, verified:** Rails 8.1 / Ruby 4.0.3 / Postgres, UUIDv7 PKs, Phlex views, Sidekiq+Redis, minitest + `fixture_kit`, rubocop with `Style/DisableSyntax` (no `unless`, no `and`/`or`, endless methods, implicit frozen literals). It's a **JJ repo** — `jj` commands, not `git`.

**Hard dependency nobody has named:** codaset has **no deploy configuration at all** — CI only, no Dockerfile/Procfile/Kamal/fly config, and `production.rb:60` still says `host: 'example.com'`. It is not deployed anywhere. Analytics ingest cannot exist before codaset ships. That is now the critical-path blocker, ahead of any client work.

questions.question:
D12 — The ingest endpoint is public and unauthenticated by nature. What stops it being abused? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-ingest-hardening>

Project/branch/task: codaset @ Rails 8.1 — a `POST /api/telemetry` that a shipped desktop app calls. It must accept requests from strangers by definition, since every install is a stranger.

ELI10: The app posts to a URL. Anyone who watches the app's network traffic sees that URL and can post to it too — a script could send a million fake events overnight and your data would be garbage with no way to tell which rows were real. The usual instinct is to hide a password in the app, but the app is a file on people's machines, so `strings` finds it in seconds and changing it means shipping a whole new version.

Stakes if we pick wrong: someone poisons the dataset and you either do not notice, or you notice and cannot separate real rows from fake ones — at which point the only fix is to throw all of it away and start over.

Recommendation: A. Rails 8 has per-controller rate limiting built in, which is the boring answer and the right one; B scores higher on paper but the extra layer is not real protection, since a secret shipped inside a binary is not a secret. Worth knowing: `rate_limit` uses `Rails.cache`, and codaset sets no `cache_store` in `production.rb`, so it would fall back to a per-machine file store — fine on one box, needs the Redis you already run for Sidekiq if it ever scales out.

Completeness: A=8/10, B=9/10, C=3/10

Pros / cons:
12A) Rails 8 built-in `rate_limit` by IP, plus strict schema validation, no auth (recommended) (human: ~3h / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Framework built-in rather than hand-rolled, so it is one line and has upstream maintenance behind it
  ✅ Strict validation is the real defence — a closed schema means garbage is rejected at the door, not at query time
  ❌ A determined attacker with rotating IPs still gets through, since nothing here proves the sender is the app
12B) Baked shared-secret header plus rate limiting (human: ~5h / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Stops trivial curl-from-a-blog-post traffic and filters accidental hits from crawlers and scanners
  ✅ Gives a cheap kill switch for one leaked version, since the server can reject a specific secret
  ❌ The secret ships inside a downloadable binary, so it is theatre, and rotating it needs a new app release
12C) No controls; filter garbage at query time (human: ~30 min / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Nothing to build, and for a tool with a few hundred installs nobody may ever bother attacking it
  ❌ A single motivated person makes the dataset worthless with no way to identify which rows to drop
  ❌ Also leaves the endpoint as an open write amplifier pointed at your own database

Net: validation is the defence that actually works; rate limiting bounds the damage; a baked secret only looks like security.

options.label: Built-in rate_limit + strict validation
options.description: Rails 8 `rate_limit to:, within:` keyed by IP, plus a closed-schema validator that rejects any unknown event name, property key, or value type. No auth. (recommended)

options.label: Baked secret header + rate limit
options.description: Adds a shared secret shipped in the app. Raises the bar past casual curl and gives a per-version kill switch. Not a real secret; rotation needs a release.

options.label: No controls, filter at query time
options.description: Accept everything, sort it out later. Nothing to build. One motivated person makes the dataset worthless.

What would you like to clarify?

Happy to go into any of it — the threat model, whether codaset is the right home given it isn't deployed, how `rate_limit` behaves without a shared cache store, or something else entirely in the plan so far.
I plan on adding licensing, so maybe now is a good time. Any new install will auto-create and register a license key with the server, which can then be used for analytics and licensing

That reframes the whole thing, and mostly in your favour. Three consequences before the question:

1. **A license key is defensible where an analytics ID was not.** Storing something on the user's device to run software they installed is a functional purpose — that's the "strictly necessary" carve-out. D3/D4 removed the install ID because it existed *only* for analytics. A license key exists for the product.
2. **The licensing channel gives you retention for free.** If every install registers and validates, the server already sees key + version + timestamp on every call. That's install counts, active installs, version spread and retention — the exact things D3 gave up — without analytics touching identity at all. Codex's "launch-weighted, not user-weighted" objection dies here.
3. **But joining them costs you the anonymity claim.** The moment an analytics row carries the license key, it's linked to a person whose record you hold. It becomes personal data: needs a lawful basis, a deletion path, and the Settings label can no longer say "anonymous."

Also new, and it needs saying: **auto-registering on install means the app phones home on first run regardless of the analytics toggle.** That has to be disclosed, or the toggle reads as covering more than it does.

D12 is void as posed — a per-install license key is a real, revocable credential, so authenticated ingest is now on the table. I'll re-ask it after this.

questions.question:
D13 — Does an analytics event carry the license key? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-license-identity-join>

Project/branch/task: codaset becomes the licensing + analytics server. Every install auto-registers a license key, so a durable per-install identity now exists for a legitimate product reason.

ELI10: You are about to have two streams reaching your server. Licensing says "install ABC123, version 2.1, checked in today" — that is who and when. Analytics says "someone opened the Files pane" — that is what. Keep them apart and each stays simple: licensing answers how many people and do they stick around, analytics answers which features get used, and neither can say what any specific person did. Staple the license key onto the analytics events and you get one joined stream that can answer far more — but every analytics row is now attached to a named customer, which changes what it legally is and what you have to promise about it.

Stakes if we pick wrong: join them and the analytics table becomes personal data — subject to deletion requests, needing a lawful basis, and the Settings toggle can no longer honestly say "anonymous". Keep them apart and you permanently cannot ask whether feature use predicts renewal, which is a genuinely valuable commercial question for a paid product.

Recommendation: A. Licensing has a real reason to know who you are because you asked for the software; analytics does not. Keeping them unjoined means the analytics rows never become personal data at all, deletion requests only ever touch one table, and you still get retention — from the licensing side, where identity belongs.

Completeness: A=7/10, B=10/10, C=9/10

Pros / cons:
13A) Never — analytics stays identity-free; retention comes from the licensing channel (recommended) (human: ~2 days / CC: ~40 min)
  ✅ Analytics rows are not personal data, so deletion, lawful basis and access requests touch only licensing
  ✅ Retention, install counts and version spread all still arrive, just through the stream that legitimately owns identity
  ❌ Cross-domain questions close permanently — you can never ask whether Files-pane users renew more often
13B) Yes — analytics carries the license key (human: ~1 day / CC: ~25 min)
  ✅ Every question is answerable, including per-customer behaviour and which features correlate with renewal
  ✅ Simplest possible implementation, since one identifier already exists and just gets attached
  ❌ Analytics becomes personal data — lawful basis, deletion path, and the "anonymous" label is no longer true
13C) Rotating pseudonym — events carry HMAC(license, secret), rotated periodically (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1h)
  ✅ Sessions and short-window behaviour become joinable without the events naming a customer directly
  ✅ Rotation bounds how far back any one pseudonym can be followed, limiting the profile it can build
  ❌ You hold the key, so it is reversible by you — regulators treat that as pseudonymous, not anonymous

Net: licensing has earned the right to identity; the question is whether analytics gets to borrow it.

options.label: Never join them
options.description: Analytics events carry no license key and no identifier. Install counts, active installs, version spread and retention are derived from licensing check-ins instead. Two streams, never joined. (recommended)

options.label: Analytics carries the license key
options.description: One identity across both. Full joins, per-customer behaviour, feature-use vs renewal. Analytics becomes personal data; "anonymous" label goes away.

options.label: Rotating pseudonym
options.description: Events carry HMAC(license key, server secret), rotated on a schedule. Joinable within a window, reversible by you, not by anyone else.

  ✅ Retention, install counts and version spread all still arrive, just through the stream that legitimately owns identity
  ❌ Cross-domain questions close permanently — you can never ask whether Files-pane users renew more often
13B) Yes — analytics carries the license key (human: ~1 day / CC: ~25 min)
  ✅ Every question is answerable, including per-customer behaviour and which features correlate with renewal
  ✅ Simplest possible implementation, since one identifier already exists and just gets attached
  ❌ Analytics becomes personal data — lawful basis, deletion path, and the "anonymous" label is no longer true
13C) Rotating pseudonym — events carry HMAC(license, secret), rotated periodically (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1h)
  ✅ Sessions and short-window behaviour become joinable without the events naming a customer directly
  ✅ Rotation bounds how far back any one pseudonym can be followed, limiting the profile it can build
  ❌ You hold the key, so it is reversible by you — regulators treat that as pseudonymous, not anonymous

Net: licensing has earned the right to identity; the question is whether analytics gets to borrow it."
  (No answer provided)

What would you like to clarify?

A few things I may have assumed wrongly, in case one of them is the sticking point:

- **Whether a license key identifies a *person* at all.** I assumed registration collects an email or ties to an account. If a license auto-creates with no personal details attached — just an opaque key minted server-side on first launch — then joining it to analytics is far less loaded than I made it sound, and option B gets much cheaper.
- **Free vs paid.** I don't know if this is licensing a paid app, or license-keys-as-install-identity for a free one. That changes both the legal framing and whether "renewal" is even a question.
- **Where the CLI sits.** You said don't track the CLI. Is it also unlicensed — free and standalone forever — or does licensing eventually cover it too?
- **Whether you want the analytics decision at all right now,** given licensing is upstream of it and codaset isn't deployed. It may be that the honest output of this review is "licensing first, analytics rides it later."

Tell me which of those is off, or ask something else.
will it make any difference if the license restricts usage? for example, max 2 projects

Yes. Three real consequences, one of which is a blocker.

**1. The CLI becomes a bypass.** This is the big one. `add-project` lives in the Go CLI. The app shells out to it, and `CommandLineInstaller` symlinks that same binary into PATH as `workroom`. So a project cap enforced in the GUI is defeated by typing `workroom add-project` in a terminal — using the tool you ship in the same bundle. Either the CLI enforces the entitlement too (it needs to read a license, handle offline, and have its own failure UX), or the cap is decorative. There's no third option while the CLI stays the engine.

That also collides with "don't track the CLI." Not tracking it is fine. Not *licensing* it is not, if limits are real.

**2. The license stops being a receipt and becomes runtime state.** A dev tool must work on a plane, so the entitlement has to be cached locally — a signed token with an expiry and a grace window. That's an offline/expiry state machine, plus clock-skew handling, plus a "your grace period expired" UX. Considerably more than "register a key on install."

**3. It *simplifies* analytics rather than complicating it.** Enforcement means the licensing side must already know the project count — you can't cap what you don't count. So project/workroom counts become licensing data, collected under a necessity basis, and analytics collecting them again would be the same fact gathered twice, once identified and once anonymously. Cleaner split:

```
licensing  →  identity, entitlement, project/workroom counts, version, check-in time
              (necessary for the product; retention + install counts fall out for free)

analytics  →  behaviour only: which panes opened, which actions run, which diff mode
              (no identity, no counts — those are licensing's job now)
```

That kills the `CountBucket` question almost entirely and makes the anonymity claim easier, not harder, because analytics no longer carries anything population-shaped.

One caution on the limit itself: `max 2 projects` on a tool whose whole premise is *isolated copies per project* will bite fast — someone with three repos hits it on day one. Workroom count is the dimension that scales with use; project count is closer to "how many repos do you own", which people don't experience as usage.

questions.question:
D13 (revised) — If the license enforces limits, does the CLI enforce them too? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-cli-entitlement-bypass>

Project/branch/task: workroom @ master — `add-project` is a Go CLI subcommand. The app drives it over `--json`, and `CommandLineInstaller` symlinks the same binary into PATH as `workroom`. You have said the CLI is never instrumented for analytics; this asks whether it is also outside licensing.

ELI10: The limit says two projects. But adding a project is done by a small command-line program, and you ship that program to everyone and put it on their PATH on purpose. So anyone who hits the limit in the app can open a terminal, type one command, and add a third project anyway — using your own tool. Either that command learns to check the license, or the limit only exists for people who never open a terminal, which for a developer tool is almost nobody.

Stakes if we pick wrong: you build licensing, enforcement, an offline grace window and a paywall UX, and the cap is bypassed by the tool in the same bundle — discovered by the first user who reads the README.

Recommendation: A. If limits are real, the engine that performs the limited action has to know about them; anything else is a cap on the GUI, not on the product. It is also the honest sequencing signal — this is a licensing project with an analytics feature attached, not the reverse.

Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10, C=8/10

Pros / cons:
13A) CLI enforces the entitlement too (recommended) (human: ~1-2 weeks / CC: ~4h)
  ✅ The cap is actually a cap, because the code that creates projects is the code that checks the limit
  ✅ One entitlement reader shared by both products, so app and CLI can never disagree about what is allowed
  ❌ Turns the standalone free CLI into licensed software, which is a real product and positioning change
13B) App-only enforcement, CLI stays unrestricted (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1h)
  ✅ Keeps the CLI free and standalone, which is its documented promise and the only option on Linux/Windows
  ❌ The limit is trivially bypassed by the binary you ship and symlink into PATH yourself
  ❌ Worse than no limit — paying users are the only ones actually constrained by it
13C) Limit workrooms rather than projects, enforced in both (human: ~1-2 weeks / CC: ~4h)
  ✅ Workroom count tracks real usage, whereas project count tracks how many repos someone happens to own
  ✅ A limit users grow into over time reads as a plan, not as a wall on day one
  ❌ Same CLI licensing change as A, plus rethinking what the tiers actually are

Net: the CLI is the engine. A limit the engine does not know about is not a limit.

input.content:
# Licensing + product analytics (Workroom app, CLI, and codaset)

## Context

This started as "what are the options for analytics in the Mac app" and turned into a licensing
project during review. That is the correct outcome, not scope creep: analytics needs an identity to
be worth much, licensing needs one for real product reasons, and once licensing exists analytics
rides it almost for free. Building analytics identity first would have been building the wrong thing.

**Where it began.** The app has no product analytics. Sentry is linked and running
(`Core/SentryConfig.swift`, started at `WorkroomApp.swift:19`) with crash reporting, hang tracking,
tracing, profiling and metrics — but it answers "what broke", never "what gets used". Nothing tells
us whether jj or git dominates, whether the inspector's Files/PR panes earn their code, or whether
the `pre` channel has anyone on it.

**Where it landed.** Every install auto-registers a license key with codaset. The license enforces
usage limits. Behaviour events carry that key, so analytics is identified data, not anonymous.
The CLI enforces the same entitlement the app does.

### The decision trail (what this review changed)

| # | Decision | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| D3 | Snapshot only, no analytics install ID | superseded by licensing — a real identity now exists |
| D4 | Self-hosted, no third-party SDK | stands — codaset is the server |
| D5 | Emit at first successful `AppStore.load`, once-flag | stands for the snapshot |
| D6 | Hoist `BuildIdentity` out of `SentryConfig` | stands |
| D7 | One in-memory retry, then drop | stands, now paired with an idempotency key |
| D8 | `CountBucket` gains `.none` | **moved to licensing** — enforcement needs exact counts, not buckets |
| D9 | Emit only on a successful load | stands |
| D10 | Snapshot **and** coarse action events | stands |
| D11 | Design the endpoint now, in `../codaset` | stands |
| D13 | The CLI enforces the entitlement too | the CLI becomes licensed software |
| D14 | Behaviour events carry the license key | analytics is personal data, with everything that implies |

## The blocker, stated plainly

**codaset is not deployed anywhere.** It has CI only — no Dockerfile, no Procfile, no Kamal or fly
config, and `config/environments/production.rb:60` still reads `host: 'example.com'`. Nothing in this
plan can ship until codaset is live. That is now the critical path, ahead of every client change.

## Architecture

```
  ┌─ Workroom.app (Swift) ──────────┐        ┌─ workroom CLI (Go) ───────────┐
  │  first launch → register        │        │  add-project → check          │
  │  behaviour events → POST        │        │  entitlement before creating  │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┘        └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │                                           │
                 │   both read the SAME cached entitlement   │
                 │   (signed token on disk, offline grace)   │
                 └─────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                   │ HTTPS, authenticated by license key
                                   ▼
              ┌─ codaset (Rails 8.1 / Postgres / Sidekiq) ─────────────┐
              │                                                        │
              │  licenses          identity, tier, limits, check-ins   │
              │    │                → install counts, retention,       │
              │    │                  version spread, project counts   │
              │    │                                                   │
              │    └──► analytics_events   license_id FK, event name,   │
              │                            typed properties, event_id   │
              │                              → behaviour, joinable      │
              └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Two tables, one identity, deliberately joined (D14). Licensing owns *who / how many / how long*;
analytics owns *what they did*. The join is what makes "which features do renewers use" answerable.

### What identified analytics costs, and must be paid

D14 traded anonymity for the renewal-correlation question. The bill:

- **The Settings toggle cannot say "anonymous."** Label it "Send usage data"; the caption must state
  plainly that it is linked to the license.
- **A privacy policy page is now required before ship**, not deferred. `website/` has none today.
- **Deletion path:** deleting or expiring a license must delete or de-identify its
  `analytics_events` rows. A foreign key with `on_delete: :cascade` is the floor.
- **Retention policy:** a fixed window with a recurring Sidekiq job that enforces it.
- **Lawful basis:** opt-out default-on for *identified* analytics is weaker than it was for
  anonymous. This is a live residual risk, flagged rather than re-litigated — it was decided
  up front and is the user's call.

## Phases

### Phase 0 — deploy codaset (blocking)

Pick a host, add deploy config, real `default_url_options`, a database, Redis for Sidekiq, and a
domain. Nothing else in this plan is reachable before this lands.

### Phase 1 — licensing server (codaset)

Rails 8.1 / Ruby 4.0.3 / Postgres, UUIDv7 PKs by default, Phlex views, minitest + `fixture_kit`.
**codaset is a JJ repo — use `jj`, not `git`.** Rubocop enforces `Style/DisableSyntax`: no `unless`,
no `and`/`or`/`not`, no numbered block params; endless methods and hash shorthand are the house style;
`# frozen_string_literal: true` is implicit and must NOT be added.

- `License` model — key, tier, limits, `last_seen_at`, org/user association.
- `POST /api/licenses` — auto-register on first launch. Returns the key plus a **signed entitlement
  token** (tier + limits + expiry) the client caches.
- `POST /api/licenses/:key/check` — periodic re-validation, refreshes the token, updates
  `last_seen_at`, records version and project/workroom counts. This is where retention, install
  counts and version spread come from.
- Rate limiting: Rails 8's built-in `rate_limit to:, within:`, keyed by license key. Note it uses
  `Rails.cache`, and codaset sets no `cache_store` in `production.rb` — point it at the Redis already
  present for Sidekiq rather than the default file store.

### Phase 2 — shared entitlement reader (Go)

One package in the `workroom` repo, consumed by **both** the CLI and (via the CLI's `--json` API) the
app. This is the D13 decision: the engine that creates projects is the engine that checks the limit.

- Verifies the signed token offline (public key baked into the binary — a *verification* key, safe to
  ship, unlike a shared secret).
- Cached token on disk with an expiry and a **grace window**, because a dev tool must work on a plane.
- Clock-skew tolerance; a clear "grace expired, reconnect to continue" state.

### Phase 3 — enforcement UX (app + CLI)

- `add-project` (and whichever action the tier actually limits) fails with a clear, actionable
  message naming the limit and how to lift it.
- The app surfaces the same state as UI, not a raw CLI error string.
- Both read one entitlement reader, so they cannot disagree about what is allowed.

### Phase 4 — analytics

**Snapshot** (D10), emitted at the end of the first *successful* `AppStore.load`
(`Core/AppStore.swift:2344`), guarded by a static once-flag. The flag is load-bearing:
`WorkroomApp.swift:54-59` documents that SwiftUI "mints one window — and one fresh `AppStore` — per
`WindowSeed`", and ⌘N opens a new seed. A failed load emits nothing and leaves the flag unset, so a
later successful reload can still emit (D9) — otherwise a broken CLI read would be recorded as a user
with no projects.

Set the flag **after** the consent check, not before, so enabling analytics later in the same process
is not permanently suppressed.

**Coarse action events** (D10) at real interaction points: inspector section opened, diff mode
switched, workroom created, VCS action run, pane split. Behaviour, not settings — the snapshot alone
measures configuration, which was Codex's sharpest hit.

**Typed payloads, no generic value container.** Codex is right that `AnalyticsValue.string(String)`
accepts any string, so a `[String: AnalyticsValue]` bag is not the compile-time guarantee the earlier
draft claimed. Each event case carries its own typed associated values — enums and integers only, no
free `String` — with an explicit wire encoder. That is what actually makes it impossible to attach a
repo path, branch, bookmark, workroom label, commit message, file name or terminal line.

**Sink.** `URLSession` POST to codaset, authenticated by the license key. Constraints:

- **`URLSessionConfiguration.ephemeral`, caching disabled.** A default session uses the shared URL
  cache, cookie storage and credential storage — a real defect Codex caught in the earlier draft.
- One in-memory retry after a short delay, then silent drop (D7). Launch is exactly when the network
  is least likely to be up (cold wake, wifi reconnecting), so a single attempt would systematically
  lose that whole category rather than a random sample.
- **A per-emit random `event_id`** (generated in memory, never persisted) sent as an idempotency key,
  with a unique index server-side. Without it the retry double-counts whenever the server accepted the
  first POST but the response was lost.
- Off the main thread. Never surfaces an error to the user.

**Counts are licensing's job now.** Enforcement cannot cap what it does not count, so project and
workroom counts arrive with the license check-in as exact numbers. Analytics does not carry them, and
`CountBucket` is not needed (D8 superseded).

### Testability — inject the seams

Codex is right that compile-time build flavour, `XCTest` env detection and global statics make
"every branch" untestable as drafted. `Analytics` takes injected **build identity**, **consent
provider**, **sink factory** and **launch-session state**, defaulting to the real ones. Same seam
`SentryConfig.defaultEnvironment(nightly:debug:)` already uses (`SentryConfig.swift:67`), and the same
reason `UITestFixture` exists.

## Files

**codaset** (JJ repo) — `app/models/license.rb`, `app/models/analytics_event.rb`,
`app/controllers/api/licenses_controller.rb`, `app/controllers/api/analytics_controller.rb`,
migrations, a retention job, deploy config, `config/routes.rb`.

**workroom CLI (Go)** — new `internal/license/` (token verify, cache, grace), enforcement in
`internal/workroom/` create paths and `cmd/add-project`.

**macapp** — `Core/BuildIdentity.swift` (hoisted from `SentryConfig`), `Core/AnalyticsEvent.swift`,
`Core/Analytics.swift`, `Core/AnalyticsHTTPSink.swift`, `Core/LicenseState.swift`; edits to
`Core/DefaultsKeys.swift`, `Core/SentryConfig.swift`, `Core/AppStore.swift:2344`,
`Views/SettingsView.swift:178`. New Swift files need `make app-generate`.

**website** — a privacy policy page, linked from the app.

## Tests

- **REGRESSION (mandatory):** hoisting `defaultEnvironment` out of `SentryConfig` modifies working
  behaviour. Moved tests keep asserting all three outputs, plus one pinning that nightly still tags
  `nightly` — that mislabelling is the documented WORKROOM-2B confusion (`SentryConfig.swift:57-63`).
- **Go:** entitlement token verify (valid / tampered / expired / clock-skewed), grace window entry and
  expiry, enforcement at the limit boundary (n-1, n, n+1), offline behaviour.
- **Rails (minitest + `fixture_kit`):** register, re-register idempotency, check-in updates
  `last_seen_at`, rate limit trips, unknown event name rejected, unknown property key rejected,
  duplicate `event_id` rejected, cascade delete removes a license's events, retention job deletes past
  the window.
- **Swift:** consent off ⇒ spy sink never called and no session constructed; debug and XCTest ⇒ noop;
  once-flag set after the consent check, not before; failed load ⇒ no emit and flag unset; every event
  case encodes to a stable name; `URLProtocol`-stubbed sink for 200 / non-2xx / transport error /
  retry-succeeds / teardown-before-retry.
- **XCUITest**, scoped to the new class only (never the full suite; `make app-uitest` ignores
  `APP_TEST_FLAGS`, so call `xcodebuild -only-testing:<Class>/<method>`): the Settings toggle flips
  and persists, matched by `accessibilityIdentifier` — XCUITest cannot match a `Form` `Toggle` by
  label.

## Failure modes

| Path | Failure | Test | Handled | User sees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Registration | Offline on first launch | yes | grace/unregistered state | clear state, app still works |
| Entitlement | Token expired, still offline | yes | grace window, then block | "reconnect to continue" |
| Entitlement | Tampered token | yes | signature verify fails | treated as unlicensed |
| Enforcement | CLI and app disagree | yes | one shared reader | n/a by construction |
| Analytics emit | Fires twice via ⌘N | yes | once-flag | nothing (correct) |
| Analytics emit | Load failed ⇒ zero counts | yes | no emit, flag unset | nothing (correct) |
| Sink | Cold wake, no wifi | yes | 1 retry, drop | nothing — silent by design |
| Sink | Response lost after accept | yes | `event_id` idempotency | nothing |
| Ingest | Flooded by a script | yes | per-key rate limit | nothing |

content.text:
Server-controlled limits and revocation mostly fit the signed-token design already — the token carries tier + limits + expiry and gets refreshed on check-in, so raising a limit is a server-side edit that lands on the next check. Three things it exposes, though:

**1. A real hole: revocation must be sticky.** As drafted, grace + revocation means a revoked user just stays offline and keeps working until the token expires. Revocation has to be written down locally the first time it's observed and never un-observed by a later offline period. Otherwise revocation is opt-in by the person being revoked.

**2. Limits going *down* is the hard case, not up.** Cut someone from 5 projects to 2 and they're over the limit with existing work on disk. That needs an explicit over-limit state in the entitlement reader that both the CLI and the app render.

**3. Token TTL is the revocation-latency dial and the offline-tolerance dial at the same time.** They're the same number pointed in opposite directions.

questions.question:
D15 — How long may a revoked license keep working offline? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-revocation-latency>

Project/branch/task: the entitlement is a signed token cached on disk with a grace window, so both the app and the CLI work on a plane. Revocation is enforced by the token expiring and not being reissued.

ELI10: The app remembers its permissions in a signed file so it works without internet. Revoking someone means refusing to renew that file — but until it expires, their copy still works. So the length of that file's life is exactly how long a revoked person keeps using the product, and it is also exactly how long an honest person can stay offline before being locked out. One number, two opposite jobs. Separately, and regardless of the number: the moment the server says "revoked", that has to be written to disk permanently, or someone can just unplug their network and keep the grace period forever.

Stakes if we pick wrong: too long and revocation is toothless for weeks; too short and a developer on a plane or behind a corporate proxy gets locked out of their own work, which is the worst possible failure for a tool that manages their source code.

Recommendation: B. A week covers essentially every genuine offline stretch — flights, conferences, a bad week of wifi — while keeping revocation meaningful. And the sticky-revocation flag matters more than the number: it turns revocation from "wait for expiry" into "immediate on first contact", which is the case that actually matters.

Completeness: A=6/10, B=9/10, C=10/10

Pros / cons:
15A) Long TTL, ~30 days (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Essentially nobody is ever locked out by being offline, which is the kindest failure mode for a dev tool
  ✅ Fewer check-ins means less server load and less to go wrong in the network path
  ❌ A revoked or refunded user keeps full access for a month, which makes revocation close to decorative
15B) Short TTL, ~7 days, plus sticky revocation (recommended) (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min)
  ✅ Covers every realistic offline stretch — flights, conferences, a bad week — without leaving a month-long hole
  ✅ Sticky revocation makes the common case immediate, since a revoked client is usually online when told
  ❌ Someone genuinely offline for more than a week gets blocked, and that person will be annoyed
15C) Short TTL plus a hard online check on launch, with a generous grace (human: ~1 week / CC: ~1h30)
  ✅ Fastest revocation and the clearest signal to the user about exactly what state they are in
  ✅ Grace is explicit and visible rather than an invisible expiry the user cannot see coming
  ❌ More states to build, test and explain, and a launch-time network dependency on the critical path

Net: one number decides both how fast revocation bites and how long an honest offline user survives.

options.label: ~7 day TTL + sticky revocation
options.description: Token lives a week; check-in refreshes it. A revocation seen once is written to disk permanently and survives going offline. Covers flights and conferences. (recommended)

options.label: ~30 day TTL
options.description: Nobody is locked out for being offline. Revoked users keep full access for up to a month.

options.label: Short TTL + launch check + visible grace
options.description: Fastest revocation, explicit user-visible grace states. More states to build and a launch-time network dependency.

questions.question:
D16 — The server cuts someone's limit from 5 projects to 2. They have 5. Now what? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-over-limit-downgrade>

Project/branch/task: server-controlled limits means limits can go down — a downgrade, an expired trial, a plan change. Raising a limit is trivial; lowering it below current usage is the case that needs a defined behaviour in the shared entitlement reader that both the CLI and the app read.

ELI10: Someone registered five repos under a plan that allowed five. Their plan changes and now allows two. Those five projects are real directories with real worktrees and real uncommitted work on their disk. The question is what the tool does on the next launch: quietly stop them adding a sixth, refuse to work until they delete three, or freeze everything until they sort it out. Only the first one leaves their existing work reachable.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a downgrade locks a developer out of source-control work they have in flight. For a tool whose entire job is managing copies of their code, that is the failure that ends the relationship — and it would land on people at their most price-sensitive moment.

Recommendation: A. B and C enforce the limit more completely, but they buy that by holding the user's own source work hostage over a billing state. That is not a tradeoff worth making for a developer tool; the limit exists to shape new usage, not to seize existing work.

Completeness: A=8/10, B=10/10, C=9/10

Pros / cons:
16A) Soft — existing projects keep working, no new ones until under the limit (recommended) (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min)
  ✅ Nobody is ever locked out of work already on their disk, whatever happens to their billing state
  ✅ The pressure to upgrade is still real and constant, since the next project they want is blocked
  ❌ Someone can sit permanently over the limit on a cheaper plan and never feel enough friction to move
16B) Hard — blocked until they remove enough projects (human: ~4 days / CC: ~1h)
  ✅ The limit means exactly what it says, with no long-lived over-limit population to reason about
  ✅ Simplest state to explain, since there is no grandfathered case in the model at all
  ❌ Forces someone to delete real workroom directories to regain access to the rest of their work
16C) Read-only until resolved (human: ~1 week / CC: ~1h30)
  ✅ Nothing is destroyed and the user can still read and copy out anything they need
  ✅ Stronger upgrade pressure than soft, without demanding deletions first
  ❌ A read-only VCS tool is barely a tool, and building a coherent read-only mode across both products is real work

Net: the limit should shape what they add next, not reach back and take what they already have.

options.label: Soft — grandfather existing
options.description: Existing projects and workrooms keep working normally. Creating a new one is blocked with a clear message until they are back under the limit. Explicit over-limit state in the shared reader. (recommended)

options.label: Hard — block until under limit
options.description: The tool refuses to operate until enough projects are removed. Limit means what it says; no grandfathered population.

options.label: Read-only until resolved
options.description: Everything readable, nothing mutable, until they are under the limit or upgrade. Nothing destroyed, strong pressure, substantial build.

Noted — going with hard block. One correction in your favour that makes it much safer than my framing implied: **"remove a project" means unregister, not delete.** `delete-project` is config-only by default (`--from-disk` is opt-in), so a blocked user drops a project from Workroom's list and their files stay untouched on disk. Two things that follow, and they're deadlock risks worth pinning with tests: while blocked, `delete-project` and `list` must **stay available** — otherwise the escape hatch is behind the wall it's meant to open — and the app must still launch and render the sidebar.

D17 / TODO — Crash reporting runs unconditionally with no user control. Capture it? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-todo-sentry-gate>

**Context for whoever picks this up:** the gate MUST wrap the `start()` call itself, not filter events afterwards. The crash handler installs before anything else can crash, which is precisely why it sits first in `init` — so it is start-or-don't, never send-or-don't. `SentryConfig.swift:16-20` documents that ordering. **Depends on:** nothing technically. Reads better shipped with the Privacy pane than alone.

Stakes if we pick wrong: skip it and the reasoning is lost — the next person to notice re-derives the start-or-don't constraint from scratch, or worse, ships an event filter that does not actually stop anything being sent.
